article.title: Midterm waves are the rule, not the exception
article.subtitle: Democrats have an increasingly large lead in the polls — and in FLIPR. But history says that shouldn’t be surprising.

extraction.summary: Model Talk arguing that FLIPR's 10.5-point projected swing toward Democrats is grounded in history. Since World War II the out-party has gained in the House popular vote in every midterm but 2002, with an average swing of 7.4 points and an interquartile range of 4.8 to 10.8. The generic ballot rose from D+6.5 to D+8.9 after Labor Day (D+9.6 among likely voters) and FLIPR's Senate odds reached 72.6 percent. A technical section explains why FLIPR's House popular vote forecast (D+7.9) is below its LV generic ballot: blending with fancy fundamentals and race polls; turnout weighting, since Republican districts have faster population growth, more eligible voters and higher turnout; replicating official tally quirks; and the fading historical prior.

findings.statement: Since World War II the party out of the White House has gained in the House popular vote in every midterm except 2002 and gained seats in all but 2002 and 1998. The average swing from the previous congressional election is 7.4 points, with an interquartile range of +4.8 to +10.8. The record is 17.4 points in 2010; 2018 was 9.7 and 2006 was 10.6.
findings.rationale: Thermostatic public opinion checks the president's power.
findings.evidence_quote: The average shift is a 7.4-point swing.

findings.statement: The magnitude of the midterm swing has been highly consistent over time even as presidential margins have narrowed, and it hits both popular and unpopular presidents, since popular presidents bring bigger coattails and have more territory to defend.
findings.evidence_quote: The magnitude of the midterm swing has been highly consistent over time, even as margins in presidential elections have diminished.

findings.statement: The generic ballot is FLIPR's single most important input but not its final answer; it feeds simple fundamentals and is blended with fancy fundamentals (including incumbency, which helps Republicans as incumbents in most seats), race-level polls (dominant in well-polled races), and in Deluxe, expert ratings calibrated to have little effect on the national vote.
findings.evidence_quote: the generic ballot is the single most important input to FLIPR, but not its “final answer”; it’s blended with lots of other data.

findings.statement: FLIPR's House popular vote forecast is the turnout-weighted sum of its 435 district forecasts. It is more Republican than a simple average because Republican districts have grown faster since the 2020 Census (FLIPR embeds a population growth model), Democratic districts have more ineligible residents (non-citizens and disenfranchised felons), turnout rises with competitiveness while safe urban seats are low-turnout, and red-state Senate races lift House turnout in those states.
findings.evidence_quote: our D +7.9 forecast is formulated by summing up FLIPR’s forecast for each district, weighted by projected turnout.

findings.statement: FLIPR replicates quirks of the official House popular vote tally: uncontested districts (including whether states count ballots in them), same-party top-two contests in California and Washington, and ranked-choice districts, where it uses the post-RCV tally in simulations where RCV is triggered. Its historical House popular vote estimates adjust for uncontested districts.
findings.evidence_quote: FLIPR tries to faithfully replicate the official tally of the House popular vote

findings.statement: FLIPR's generic ballot estimate is a 'now-cast'. Classic and Deluxe blend in a prior from midterm history since World War II conditioned on presidential approval and other factors, with influence fading to zero by Election Day; in late September 2026 the prior and the current estimate were very close.
findings.evidence_quote: the prior’s influence on the model fades to zero by Election Day.

findings.statement: Forecasts that start near 50/50 tend to have bigger probability swings than lopsided ones for the same change in fundamentals, which is why FLIPR's Senate odds (to 72.6 percent) moved more than its House odds.
findings.evidence_quote: forecasts that start out near 50/50 tend to have bigger probability swings.

findings.statement: Silver says Silver Bulletin/FiveThirtyEight forecasts have essentially never been on the opposite side of the conventional wisdom; differences have been in degree of confidence: more cautious than consensus about Clinton in 2016, and confident that Biden's 2020 lead could withstand a 2016-sized polling error, which it did even though 2020 polls were more biased.
findings.evidence_quote: general election polls were actually more biased in 2020 than in 2016, but Biden’s lead was big enough to absorb the blow.

findings.statement: Between Sept. 7 and Sept. 29, 2026 the generic ballot moved from D+6.5 to D+8.9, about 2.5 points, larger than the post-Labor Day swing in most recent midterms. FLIPR's launch odds on Aug. 11 were about 55 percent for the Senate and 85 percent for the House, within a few points of prediction markets, which FLIPR's publication itself influenced.
findings.evidence_quote: On Sept. 7, they led by 6.5 points; now that lead has expanded to 8.9 points.

political_insights.insight: Midterm backsliding for the president's party is perhaps the most durable trend in American politics, driven by thermostatic opinion and perceived overreach (1946, 1966, 1974, 1994, 2010).
political_insights.forecasting_implication: A strong prior toward out-party gains is justified even without polls.

political_insights.insight: Before 1994, Democratic House dominance rested on a coalition of Northern liberals and Southern populists; realignments in 1972, 1980, 1994, 2010 and 2016 moved rural and Southern white voters to Republicans.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Pre-1994 House data reflect a different party system; weight recent data more.

political_insights.insight: Only four Republican senators hold true swing states, and the Senate's equal apportionment by state is what keeps Republican hopes alive in a strong Democratic year.
political_insights.forecasting_implication: Senate outcomes depend heavily on which seats are up.

references.description: Nate Cohn analysis of midterm swings from previous congressional election

open_questions: Details of FLIPR's embedded population growth model.
